title: Amdahl's Law Fundamentals
summary: The canonical law bounding parallel speedup — why the serial fraction of a program, not the number of processors, sets the ceiling.

slides.subTitle: Speedup is capped by what can't be sped up
slides.markdown:
**Amdahl's Law** says: if a fraction `p` of a program's work can be sped up (e.g. parallelized) and the rest, `1-p`, cannot, then no matter how much you speed up the `p` portion, the *overall* speedup is bounded by how large `1-p` is.

The intuition: the serial part runs at the same speed no matter what you do to the rest, so it becomes an ever-larger share of total time as the parallel part shrinks toward zero. Eventually the serial part alone dominates, and further parallelism buys almost nothing.

slides.subTitle: speedup = 1 / ((1-p) + p/s)
slides.markdown:
`p` = the fraction of work that can be sped up; `s` = the speedup factor applied to that fraction (e.g. `s=4` on 4 processors, ideally). The remaining `(1-p)` fraction still takes the same time it always did.

Overall speedup = `1 / ((1-p) + p/s)`. As `s -> infinity` (perfect, unlimited parallelism on the parallel part), the `p/s` term vanishes and speedup approaches `1/(1-p)` — a hard ceiling set entirely by the serial fraction, explored next.

slides.subTitle: Speedup vs processor count
slides.markdown:
Plotting speedup against processor count for several serial fractions shows the same shape every time.

![A speedup-vs-processor-count curve for several serial fractions, showing the ceiling](assets/amdahl-speedup-curves.svg)

Each curve rises quickly at first, then flattens hard — the flat asymptote is exactly `1/(1-p)`. A smaller serial fraction pushes the ceiling higher, but every curve still has one.

assets.alt: A speedup-vs-processor-count curve for several serial fractions, showing the ceiling

slides.subTitle: A worked example
slides.markdown:
```text
A program is 80% parallelizable (p = 0.8), running on 10 processors
with ideal per-processor speedup (s = 10) on the parallel portion.

speedup = 1 / ((1 - 0.8) + 0.8/10)
        = 1 / (0.2 + 0.08)
        = 1 / 0.28
        ~= 3.57x

Even with 10 processors, you get well under 10x — the 20% serial
part alone caps the achievable speedup far below the processor count.
```

slides.subTitle: Infinite processors still can't beat 1/(1-p)
slides.markdown:
Take the parallel speedup `s` to infinity — imagine infinite processors, each instruction in the parallel part executing in zero time. Overall speedup still only approaches `1/(1-p)`, never exceeding it.

With `p = 0.8` (80% parallelizable), that ceiling is `1/0.2 = 5x` — no matter how much hardware you throw at it. This is why reducing the *serial fraction itself* (algorithmic change, not more cores) is often the higher-leverage move once a program is already substantially parallelized.

slides.subTitle: Amdahl's Law vs Gustafson's Law
slides.markdown:
| | Amdahl's Law | Gustafson's Law |
|---|---|---|
| Assumption | Fixed total workload; more processors just finish it faster | Workload grows with available processors — bigger problems get tackled, not the same problem faster |
| Implication | Speedup is bounded by the serial fraction, however small | Speedup can scale much closer to linear, because the serial part shrinks as a fraction of a bigger total job |

**How to decide:** Amdahl's framing fits fixed-size, latency-bound tasks (make this one job finish faster). Gustafson's framing fits throughput-bound tasks where more hardware means tackling a proportionally larger problem in the same time (e.g. scientific simulations at higher resolution) — a very different real-world question, not a contradiction of Amdahl's math.

slides.subTitle: The wrong "p"
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "90% of my algorithm's *instructions* are parallelizable, so p = 0.9 in Amdahl's Law."

**Why it's wrong:** `p` must capture the **entire** serial cost, including synchronization and coordination overhead — not just instructions that could theoretically run independently. Locks and data shuffling are serial-equivalent costs a naive instruction count misses, and often dominate at high processor counts.

**Correct model:** measure `p` empirically from wall-clock behavior, not a static instruction count — the real serial fraction is almost always larger than it looks.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: why buying more cores stops paying off
slides.subTitle: Diminishing returns as processor count grows
slides.markdown:
A workload with p = 0.95 (95% parallelizable), evaluated at increasing processor counts (s = processor count, ideal per-processor speedup):

```
processors=4:    speedup = 1 / (0.05 + 0.95/4)   = 1 / 0.2875  ~= 3.48x
processors=16:   speedup = 1 / (0.05 + 0.95/16)  = 1 / 0.1094  ~= 9.14x
processors=64:   speedup = 1 / (0.05 + 0.95/64)  = 1 / 0.0648  ~= 15.4x
processors=1024: speedup = 1 / (0.05 + 0.95/1024) = 1 / 0.0509 ~= 19.6x
ceiling (s -> infinity): 1 / 0.05 = 20x
```

Going from 4 to 16 processors (4x more hardware) buys a 2.6x speedup gain. Going from 64 to 1024 processors (16x more hardware) buys barely 4.2x. This is exactly why massively multicore systems eventually stop paying for themselves on a fixed workload — the returns on each additional processor shrink fast once you're within a small factor of the 1/(1-p) ceiling, and no amount of additional hardware pushes past it.

slides.sectionTitle: Finding the serial fraction in practice
slides.subTitle: Where p actually comes from in real systems
slides.markdown:
In real systems, the serial fraction `(1-p)` usually isn't a clean algorithmic property — it's whatever forces threads to wait on each other: a global lock protecting shared state, a single-writer log, a barrier every thread must reach before proceeding, or a setup/teardown phase that can't be split. Profiling a real multithreaded system for Amdahl's-Law purposes means measuring **time spent contended or blocked**, not just counting how many lines of code look parallel.

This is precisely why reducing lock contention (finer-grained locks, lock-free structures, sharding shared state) is one of the highest-leverage performance changes available on a many-core system — it directly shrinks `(1-p)`, which raises the *ceiling* every other optimization is bounded by, rather than just speeding up work that was already going to scale.
